title: Dynamics
standard_text: Motion in two dimensions and projectiles; Newton's laws with free-body diagrams, inclines, friction and connected objects; uniform circular motion, centripetal acceleration and centripetal force; and frames of reference. (summary of The Ontario Curriculum, Grades 11 and 12: Science (2008), Physics, Grade 12, University Preparation (SPH4U), Strand B: Dynamics)
meta_desc: Free Grade 12 Physics (SPH4U) worksheets on dynamics: projectiles, forces on inclines, friction, pulleys and elevators, uniform circular motion and centripetal force. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Resolve forces into components and apply Fnet = ma along each direction.
key_sub: Circular motion: ac = v²/r towards the centre.
body_html:
How to think about it

Treat projectile motion as two independent motions: constant horizontal velocity and a vertical acceleration of 9.8 m/s² downwards. On an incline, split the weight into mg sin θ along the slope and mg cos θ into the slope; the normal force balances mg cos θ.

An object moving in a circle at constant speed accelerates towards the centre: ac = v²/r = 4π²r/T². The centripetal force Fc = mv²/r is not a new force; it is provided by tension, friction, gravity or a normal force.

Example

A 1000 kg car rounds a curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s. Centripetal force?

F = mv²/r = 1000 × 400 ÷ 50

Answer: 8000 N

Example

A box slides down a frictionless 30° ramp. Acceleration?

a = g sin 30°

Answer: 4.9 m/s²

Common mistakes

  • Drawing a 'centrifugal' force outwards on a free-body diagram.
  • Using mg instead of mg cos θ for the normal force on a ramp.
  • Letting the horizontal velocity of a projectile change.

faq.q: What keeps a satellite in orbit?
faq.a: Gravity supplies the centripetal force that keeps it turning.

faq.q: Why do you feel heavier in an elevator that accelerates upwards?
faq.a: The floor must push up with more than your weight to give you an upward acceleration.

items.q: A body is in equilibrium. What is the net force on it?
A force of 20 N acts at 65° above the horizontal. Calculate its vertical component.
A force of 40 N acts at 55° above the horizontal. Calculate its vertical component.
A uniform beam is balanced on a pivot at its centre. A 10 N weight hangs 0.25 m to the left of the pivot. What weight must hang 0.50 m to the right to balance it?
items.e: Principle of moments: 10 × 0.25 = W × 0.50, W = 5.00 N.

items.q: A uniform beam is balanced on a pivot at its centre. A 6 N weight hangs 0.40 m to the left of the pivot. What weight must hang 0.15 m to the right to balance it?
items.e: Principle of moments: 6 × 0.40 = W × 0.15, W = 16.0 N.

items.q: What force gives a 10 kg body an acceleration of 0.500 m/s²?
Why do passengers fall forward when a bus stops suddenly?
items.e: The body tends to keep moving.

items.q: What force gives a 1000 kg body an acceleration of 4 m/s²?
A horse pulls a cart. Why does the cart move if the cart pulls the horse back equally?
c: the forces act on different bodies; friction from the ground pushes the horse forward
items.e: Consider forces on each body separately.

items.q: Why are roads banked on curves?
c: a part of the normal force provides centripetal force
items.e: tan θ = v²/(rg) for no friction.
